artiest/van-morrison.text:
Van Morrison is a Northern Irish singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist, born in 1945 in Belfast, the only child of a shipyard electrician and a mother who had been a singer and tap dancer. His father had one of the largest record collections in Northern Ireland, with blues, gospel, jazz and folk. Van Morrison played guitar, harmonica, keyboards and saxophone in showbands before becoming, in the mid-1960s, the singer of the Belfast R&B band Them. With them he wrote and recorded Gloria, a standard for garage bands. His solo career began in 1967 with Brown Eyed Girl, under the guidance of producer Bert Berns.

After Berns's death, Warner Bros. bought his contract and gave him three sessions for Astral Weeks (1968). The album sold poorly at first, but is now regarded as a classic. Moondance (1970) made him a major name, and in the 1970s highly acclaimed albums and live performances followed. More than forty albums have reached the British top 40.

Much of his music follows the forms of soul and early rhythm and blues. Another part consists of long, spiritually inspired musical journeys influenced by the Celtic tradition, jazz and associative storytelling, such as Astral Weeks. Together these strands are sometimes called Celtic soul. Morrison was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame, received two Grammys and was knighted in 2016.
artiest/van-morrison.listen: Listen to Astral Weeks and notice how the voice floats freely above the acoustic accompaniment. Can you hear how the story is more a mood than an anecdote?

artiest/vandenberg.text:
Vandenberg is a Dutch hard rock band from Amsterdam, formed in 1981 and named after guitarist Adriaan van den Berg, who calls himself Adrian Vandenberg internationally. He brought in singer Bert Heerink, bassist Dick Kemper and drummer Jos Zoomer. A demo ended up with the journalist Kees Baars, who became manager and placed the group with Atlantic Records. The debut album Vandenberg was recorded at the Sol Studios of Jimmy Page, the former guitarist of Led Zeppelin.

The 1983 single Burning Heart also did well in America. Heading for a Storm followed, with Different Worlds, and in 1985 Alibi, produced by Jaap Eggermont, the former drummer of Golden Earring. The band toured the United States as the support act for Ozzy Osbourne and Kiss and played Japan on its own in 1984. Alibi did not make the charts and Heerink left the group.

In 1987 David Coverdale asked Vandenberg to be Whitesnake's permanent guitarist, after he had already played as a guest soloist. He accepted, because his own band had little success. In 2020 he used the name again for a new line-up, with the album 2020, and in 2023 with Sin. The music of Vandenberg is melodic hard rock with heavy guitar riffs, multi-voice vocal parts and choruses that seemed made for American radio. In the Nederpop of School of Rock, the band shows that Dutch rock could also sound right for the American market.
artiest/vandenberg.listen: Listen to Burning Heart by Vandenberg. Notice the guitar riff and the chorus that seems made to be sung along to on the radio.

artiest/vangelis.text: Vangelis, born Evangelos Papathanassiou, was a Greek musician who was largely self-taught. He first became known with the rock group Aphrodite's Child and afterwards worked from his own studio in London. He often performed the music himself, live on synthesizers, without a score written out in advance. His music for Chariots of Fire (1981) combines a simple piano melody with warm synthesizer chords. It won an Oscar. For Ridley Scott's Blade Runner (1982) he created a dark, floating sound with synthesizer, saxophone and reverb. That atmosphere became the model for a great deal of science fiction. Later came, among others, 1492: Conquest of Paradise (1992).
artiest/vangelis.listen: Notice the broad, slowly swelling synthesizer chords with plenty of reverb, and the simple melodies above them.

artiest/vassilis-tsitsanis.text:
Vassilis Tsitsanis was a Greek composer and bouzouki player, born in 1915 in Trikala. He is regarded as one of the founders of modern rebetiko and laiko. In total he wrote more than five hundred songs. His family came from Epirus, and his colleagues sometimes called him the Vlach, because he was the only rebetiko player of his time who came from the mainland and not from the islands. From an early age he played violin, mandola and mandolin, instruments that recur in many of his songs.

In 1936 he went to Athens to study law. A year later he had also learned to play the bouzouki and made his first recording. In 1938 he moved to Thessaloniki, where he did his military service and stayed for about ten years, including during the German occupation. There he became famous, opened an ouzeri, married and wrote many of his best songs. By the time the occupier closed the record companies in 1941, he had already recorded about a hundred songs of his own.

In 1946 he returned to Athens and recorded many of his own compositions, which made singers such as Sotiria Bellou, Marika Ninou, Ioanna Georgakopoulou and Prodromos Tsaousakis famous. He developed the Westernisation of rebetiko, brought it to large parts of the population and thus laid the foundation for the later laiko. He was a friend of Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou. On his sixty-ninth birthday in 1984 he died in London after a lung operation. All of Greece mourned.
artiest/vassilis-tsitsanis.listen: Listen to a song by Tsitsanis and notice the bright, plucked sound of the bouzouki. Can you hear how the instrument follows and answers the vocal melody?

artiest/vassilis-tsitsanis-en-marika-nin.text:
Vassilis Tsitsanis was born in 1915 in Trikala and is regarded as one of the founders of modern rebetiko and laiko. He played the bouzouki and wrote more than five hundred songs. As a child he learned violin, mandola and mandolin. In 1936 he left for Athens to study law, and a year later he learned to play the bouzouki and made his first recording. In 1938 he moved to Thessaloniki, where he stayed for ten years, opened an ouzeri and wrote many of his best songs during the German occupation. By 1941 he had already recorded some hundred songs of his own.

In 1946 he returned to Athens and recorded his own compositions with male and female singers, among them Sotiria Bellou and Marika Ninou. His songs made the singers famous. Tsitsanis Westernised rebetiko a little and brought it to a wide public, thereby laying the foundation for the later laiko. Ninou was one of the voices that carried his songs.

He died in London in 1984, on his sixty-ninth birthday, and was commemorated throughout Greece. The bouzouki, which in his hands could sound both cheerful and melancholy, became the hallmark of Greek song.
artiest/vassilis-tsitsanis-en-marika-nin.listen: Listen to Synnefiasmeni Kyriaki and notice the bouzouki and Ninou's voice. Can you hear how the song sounds melancholy and yet has a melody you keep singing along to?

artiest/ved-vrind-priesters-uit-varanasi.text:
Ved Vrind is a group of priests from Varanasi, one of the holiest cities of Hinduism, on the Ganges, who recite the Vedas. No source was found about the group itself, so this text mainly describes the tradition they continue. The Rigveda is one of the oldest sacred texts of India. It consists of hymns that for centuries were not written down but passed on orally from teacher to pupil. The correct pronunciation and pitch of every syllable are regarded as essential.

To preserve the text without error, various ways of reciting it arose, the paath. In the Samhita Paath the text is sung in its normal, continuous form. The Ghana Paath is much more complicated: words are repeated back and forth in a fixed order and interlocked with one another, so that every part of the hymn sounds several times and a mistake is noticed at once. It is an extremely precise memory system.

The sound is that of a single voice, with a small range of notes, sung in a regular rhythm and without accompaniment. There is no melody in the ordinary sense, but a fixed pattern of high and low sounds. In School of Rock, two recordings from 2015 belong to the oldest forms of sung music that are still passed on as a living tradition.
artiest/ved-vrind-priesters-uit-varanasi.listen: Listen to Samhita Paath and then to Ghana Paath. Notice the single-voice singing without instruments and hear how the second recording repeats the same words again and again in a different pattern.

artiest/venice-baroque-orchestra.text:
The Venice Baroque Orchestra is a Baroque orchestra founded in 1997 by the Italian conductor and harpsichordist Andrea Marcon. It is based in Venice. In 2019 it performed in the summer series of the Naumburg Orchestral Concerts, in the Naumburg Bandshell in Central Park in New York.

The titles of the albums show what the orchestra concentrates on: the music of Antonio Vivaldi and other composers of the Venetian Baroque. The first recording was released in 1998 and contained unpublished concertos and cantatas from a manuscript in Venice. In 2000 came The Four Seasons with three violin concertos, followed by, among others, Late Violin Concertos (2001), L'arte del violino (2002), Late Vivaldi Concertos (2002) and Concerto veneziano (2005). The orchestra also recorded vocal music: Arias (2002), Andromeda Liberata (2004), Ah! mio cor: Handel Arias (2007) and Amor sacro: Vivaldi mottetti (2007).

The list of recordings shows that the orchestra plays both instrumental and vocal music, from violin concertos to arias and motets. It is thus an example of a contemporary ensemble that spreads the Venetian Baroque repertoire mainly through recordings and tours.
artiest/venice-baroque-orchestra.listen: Listen to a movement from The Four Seasons as performed by the Venice Baroque Orchestra and notice the fast strings and the changing tempo. Which season do you hear?

artiest/vernon-reid.text:
Vernon Reid was born in London in 1958 to parents from Montserrat. A year later the family moved to New York, where he attended Brooklyn Technical High School and New York University. In the 1980s he came to prominence as a guitarist in The Decoding Society, Ronald Shannon Jackson's avant-garde jazz-rock band. In 1984 he made the duo album Smash & Scatteration with Bill Frisell. In 1985, together with the journalist Greg Tate and the producer Konda Mason, he founded the Black Rock Coalition.

That group consisted of Black musicians who felt that rock belonged to them just as much. Reid himself founded Living Colour in 1984, with a stable line-up from 1986. The debut album Vivid from 1988 went double platinum. Time's Up from 1990 went gold, and the band won a Grammy for best hard rock performance two years in a row. Living Colour supported the Rolling Stones in 1989 and played the first Lollapalooza in 1991. The group split up in 1995 and reunited in 2000.

Reid's guitar playing blends heavy metal and punk with funk, R&B and avant-garde jazz, often with lightning-fast solos. In 1996 he made the solo album Mistaken Identity, worked with choreographers such as Bill T. Jones and produced, among others, Salif Keita and James Blood Ulmer. Rolling Stone ranked him high on its list of the greatest guitarists of all time. For School of Rock he is important above all as a voice in the conversation about who belongs in rock.
artiest/vernon-reid.listen: Listen to Cult of Personality by Living Colour. Notice the guitar of Vernon Reid, which sounds far from a standard rock solo, and how hard and funky the band plays together.

artiest/vic-flick.text:
Vic Flick was an English session guitarist, one of the busiest in London in the 1960s, and best known for the guitar riff in the James Bond Theme. He was born in 1937 in Worcester Park, Surrey, the son of a piano teacher and a singer. At fourteen he began playing guitar in his father's dance band. In the 1950s he played in bands at Butlin's holiday camps, was asked by bandleader Eric Winstone to play for BBC radio, and toured with the Bob Cort Skiffle Group and Paul Anka. After that he joined the John Barry Seven, and wrote Zapata, a hit from 1961.

In 1963 he left the group and grew into one of London's most important session guitarists. He played the lead guitar in the James Bond Theme on the soundtrack of Dr. No and continued to work on Bond films well into the 1980s. His guitar can be heard on records by Dusty Springfield, Nancy Sinatra, Cliff Richard and Shirley Bassey, on all of Tom Jones's early hits, such as It's Not Unusual and What's New Pussycat?, and on Petula Clark's Downtown. With Herman's Hermits he played the riff in Silhouettes. With the George Martin Orchestra he played the solo in Ringo's Theme (This Boy) in the Beatles film A Hard Day's Night, and on Paul McCartney's Thrillington.

He also wrote music for Merchant Ivory films, such as Heat and Dust. In 2012 he was honoured by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, and he died in 2024. Flick shows how a studio musician defines the sound of an era without appearing on the sleeve.
artiest/vic-flick.listen: Listen to the James Bond Theme and notice the electric guitar riff, low, sharp and menacing. How often does it return?

artiest/vicki-anderson.text:
Vicki Anderson, born Myra Barnes in 1939 in Houston, Texas, was an American soul singer, best known for her performances with the James Brown Revue. She recorded a number of singles under both her birth name and her stage name. In 1965 she joined Brown, replacing Anna King. For three years she was his leading female singer, until Marva Whitney replaced her in 1968. When Whitney left, she returned in 1969 and stayed for three more years, until Lyn Collins took her place in 1972. Brown wrote in his autobiography that Anderson was the best singer he ever had in his revue.

In 1970 she released the funk song The Message from the Soul Sisters. In 1975 a single followed on Brown's label I-Dentify under the name Momie-O, with a cover of Rufus's Once You Get Started and Bobby Womack's Stop On By. In the late 1980s she toured Britain with the James Brown Funky People Revue, and in the mid-1990s with her husband Bobby Byrd, the founder of The Famous Flames, whom she had married in the mid-1960s. Their daughter Carleen Anderson became a singer herself and has released albums in Britain since the 1990s. Vicki Anderson died in 2023 at the age of 83. She shows how large the role of female singers was in the revue of the man who invented funk.
artiest/vicki-anderson.listen: Listen to The Message from the Soul Sisters and notice Anderson's voice above the tight, rhythmic funk playing. How powerful, or how restrained, does she sound?

artiest/victor-herbert.text:
Victor Herbert was an American composer, cellist and conductor of English and Irish descent and with a German education. He was born in 1859 on Guernsey, grew up in Stuttgart and at first wanted to become a doctor, but chose music for lack of money. He studied cello with Bernhard Cossmann and at the Stuttgart Conservatoire, and by the age of nineteen was already playing as a soloist with major German orchestras. In 1886 he moved with his wife, the opera singer Therese Förster, to the United States, where both worked at the Metropolitan Opera.

Herbert was a cello soloist, conductor and teacher, and also composed a great deal. His Cello Concerto No. 2 in E minor from 1894 entered the standard repertoire. From 1898 to 1904 he conducted the Pittsburgh Symphony, after which he founded the Victor Herbert Orchestra. He became best known for his operettas for Broadway, from 1894. Successes were The Serenade (1897), The Fortune Teller (1898), Babes in Toyland (1903), Mlle. Modiste (1905), The Red Mill (1906), Naughty Marietta (1910), Sweethearts (1913) and Eileen (1917). In total he wrote 43 operettas, two operas and a great deal of orchestral, cello and piano music.

He also belonged to the Tin Pan Alley composers and was one of the founders of ASCAP, the organisation that looks after composers' rights. After the First World War tastes changed and he wrote musicals, but he did not repeat his great successes. He died in 1924. Herbert brought the European operetta tradition to the American theatre.
artiest/victor-herbert.listen: Listen to a melody from Babes in Toyland and notice the light, danceable tone of the operetta. Which song stays in your head the longest?

artiest/victor-young.text: Victor Young was born in Chicago in 1899 and had violin lessons from the age of six. He studied at the Warsaw Conservatoire and played there as a violinist in the Philharmonic Orchestra. Back in America he worked as a violinist and arranger in theatre and dance orchestras. At Paramount he wrote music for a long series of films, such as For Whom the Bell Tolls (1943). The Quiet Man (1952) and the western Shane (1953) are also his. He wrote songs that became jazz standards, such as Stella by Starlight and When I Fall in Love. Young was nominated for an Oscar 22 times. He won only after his death, for Around the World in 80 Days (1956).
artiest/victor-young.listen: Notice the songlike melodies in the violins: Young thinks like a songwriter, and every theme could also exist as a song.

artiest/victoria-beckham.text:
Victoria Beckham was born Victoria Adams in 1974 in Harlow, Essex, and grew up in Hertfordshire. After seeing the musical film Fame in 1980, she decided to go into music. She studied dance and modelling at Laine Theatre Arts in Epsom. In the 1990s she became known as a member of the Spice Girls, in which she was called Posh Spice. The group came out of auditions and, after a change shortly afterwards, consisted of five singers: Geri Halliwell, Melanie Brown, Emma Bunton, Melanie Chisholm and Victoria Adams.

After the Spice Girls split up in 2000, she signed to Virgin Records and in 2001 released her first solo album, Victoria Beckham, with two singles in the British top ten. Her solo career as a singer remained limited to that. She married the footballer David Beckham and appeared in a series of television documentaries, including Being Victoria Beckham in 2002 and a Netflix documentary in 2025.

In 2008 she started a fashion label of her own, which in 2011 was named designer brand of the year in England. She grew into an internationally recognised style icon and in 2017 received an honour as Officer of the Order of the British Empire. Her career shows how a pop group from the 1990s could produce a household name that reaches far beyond music.
artiest/victoria-beckham.listen: Listen to a single by the Spice Girls, such as Wannabe. Notice how the singers take turns singing a line and how you can hear each voice playing a role of its own.

artiest/vienna-art-orchestra.text:
The Vienna Art Orchestra was a European jazz group from Vienna, organised alternately as a big band and as a smaller combo. The group was regarded as one of the most important jazz ensembles in Europe and was an official cultural ambassador of Austria. It was founded in 1977 by Mathias Rüegg, who was its leader and composer. At first the orchestra played its postmodern compositions on stages across Europe. The founders included singer Lauren Newton, saxophonists Wolfgang Puschnig and Harry Sokal, trombonist Christian Radovan, tuba player Jon Sass and drummer Woody Schabata.

In 1980 the group signed to the Swiss label hatART, and in 1984 it toured the United States for the first time. At the end of the 1980s the orchestra paused for a while. In 1992 a new period began with fewer musicians. The group then played less of Rüegg's work and concentrated on arrangements of Duke Ellington, Charles Mingus and other American jazz composers, alongside music inspired by Verdi, Wagner, Schubert and Erik Satie. In 1997 the line-up changed again, with more and younger musicians and new compositions by Rüegg, often in concerts with images and staging.

The orchestra gave more than eight hundred concerts and released more than thirty-five recordings. In 1998 the film An Echo from Europe: Vienna Art Orchestra on Tour was released. For All That Strauss (2001) and Art and Fun (2003) it was nominated for an Amadeus Austrian Music Award. In 2010 Rüegg disbanded the orchestra for financial reasons.
artiest/vienna-art-orchestra.listen: Listen to a recording by the Vienna Art Orchestra of music by Duke Ellington and notice what the band adds that you do not hear in the original.

artiest/vijay-benedict.text:
Vijay Benedict is a former Indian playback singer in Bollywood film. He was born in Allahabad, in a North Indian Christian family, studied in Prayagraj in Uttar Pradesh and earned a degree in business administration. Playback singers record the songs, after which the actors lip-sync them in the film.

His breakthrough came in 1982 with the film Disco Dancer. He sang the title song I Am a Disco Dancer for the actor Mithun Chakraborty. The director was Babbar Subhash and the musical direction was by Bappi Lahiri. After that he was often used for films with the same actor, director and composer. He also worked with Laxmikant Pyarelal, Anand and Milind and Nadeem and Shravan and sang for actors such as Govinda, Jackie Shroff and Aamir Khan. He sang duets with, among others, Asha Bhosle, Alisha Chinai and Kumar Sanu. In total he sang for more than thirty-five films, between 1982 and 1992.

In 1991 his brother was murdered in Germany by a mafia gang. After that he stopped playback singing and devoted himself to his faith as a gospel singer. He has remained best known as the voice of the disco fashion in Indian film of the 1980s.
artiest/vijay-benedict.listen: Listen to I Am a Disco Dancer and notice the synthesizers and the danceable beat. Can you hear how the voice adds an almost theatrical, infectious energy?

artiest/viji-subramaniam.text:
Viji Subramaniam, also known as Viji Shankar, was an Indian singer, born in 1952 as Vijayashree Shankar in Madras and raised in Bombay. She was the daughter of the singer Lakshmi Shankar and Rajendra Shankar, the older brother of the sitar player Ravi Shankar. Like her mother and uncle, she was trained in both Hindustani and South Indian classical music. From a young age she accompanied her mother at concerts, often on tambura as well. In 1972 she won the President of India medal from All India Radio. Ravi Shankar described her voice in his autobiography Raga Mala as sweet and lovely.

In 1974 she joined, together with her aunt Kamala Chakravarty and her mother, Shankar's Music Festival from India, a revue sponsored by George Harrison. She sang on the studio album Ravi Shankar's Music Festival from India (1976), produced by Harrison at his estate Friar Park, and went on the North American tour in late 1974. During that festival she met the violinist L. Subramaniam, whom she married in 1976. Together they devised Global Music, an idea to reduce the dominance of Western music, written for an orchestra of a hundred musicians.

For the director Mira Nair she composed and sang music for Salaam Bombay! (1988) and Mississippi Masala (1991). In 1992 she started the Lakshminarayana Global Music Festival with her husband. She died of cancer in 1995.
artiest/viji-subramaniam.listen: Listen to a recording by Viji Subramaniam and notice the way the singing follows the rhythm of the tambura. How does she sing the long lines of the melody?

artiest/vikingur-olafsson.text:
Víkingur Ólafsson is an Icelandic pianist, born in 1984. He grew up in Reykjavik and had his first piano lessons from his mother, who was a piano teacher. Later he studied at the Juilliard School in New York. In 2011 he was the soloist at the opening concert of the Harpa concert hall in Reykjavik, playing Grieg's piano concerto under the baton of Vladimir Ashkenazy. He has played with major orchestras such as the Berliner Philharmoniker, the New York Philharmonic and the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, and has given six piano concertos by Icelandic composers their premieres.

His first albums, including Debut (2009) and Winterreise (2012), were released on his own label Dirrindí. In 2016 he signed to Deutsche Grammophon. His album Philip Glass Piano Works (2017) brought him a great deal of attention, and The New York Times called him Iceland's Glenn Gould. The next album, Johann Sebastian Bach (2018), won, among other awards, BBC Music Magazine's Album of the Year, and in 2019 he became Gramophone's Artist of the Year. Debussy • Rameau (2020), Mozart & Contemporaries (2021) and Opus 109 (2025) followed. He also made Bach Reworks, with arrangements of Bach by, among others, Ben Frost.

In 2023 he began a world tour to play a single work, Bach's Goldberg Variations, 88 times. The recording of it won a Grammy in 2025. He also collaborated with Philip Glass and Björk. He shows how far a classical pianist can reach a new audience with old and new music.
artiest/vikingur-olafsson.listen: Listen to the aria with which his recording of the Goldberg Variations begins and notice how calmly and evenly he plays. What changes in the next variation?

artiest/viktor-tsoi.text:
Viktor Tsoi was born in 1962 in Leningrad, today's St Petersburg, the son of a Russian mother and a Korean father from Kazakhstan. He began writing songs as a teenager and from 1974 to 1977 played in the school band Palata No. 6. Later he followed an art course. He was a singer and songwriter, painter and actor, and co-founded Kino. In the autumn of 1981 that band became a member of the Leningrad Rock Club, a place where music could exist outside the official channels.

Kino grew into one of the most popular and influential groups in Russian music history. After the film Assa in 1987, in which the band performed, its popularity shot up, a period that was called Kinomania. In 1988 Tsoi played the lead role in the film The Needle. He made ten albums. In 1990 he gave a major concert in the Luzhniki Stadium in Moscow. Two months later he was killed in a traffic accident, on 15 August 1990.

Tsoi is regarded as one of the pioneers of rock music in Russia and he made the genre popular throughout the Soviet Union. His songs combine simple melodies with lyrics that feel philosophical. Later, too, recordings of him appeared with only his voice and guitar, such as Akusticheskiy kontsert from 1994. In School of Rock's story of rock behind the Iron Curtain, he is the face of a generation that expressed itself through music.
artiest/viktor-tsoi.listen: Listen to a recording of Viktor Tsoi with only voice and acoustic guitar, for example from Akusticheskiy kontsert. Notice how little is needed to carry the song.

artiest/vilayat-khan.text:
Vilayat Khan was born in 1928 in Gouripur, in present-day Bangladesh, and died in 2004. He came from a family of sitar players: his father Enayat Khan and his grandfather Imdad Khan were famous. His father died when he was ten, so he was taught by his uncle, his maternal grandfather and his mother. As a boy he wanted to become a singer, but his mother felt that he should continue the family tradition on the sitar. He made his first record when he was eight. He gave his last concert at the age of seventy-five.

Khan is regarded as one of the greatest sitarists of his time. He helped develop the gayaki ang, a style of playing in which the sitar imitates the singing voice, so that the instrument almost seems to sing. He invented a technique for bending the note after plucking the string. He improvised a great deal and liked to play without the tanpura drone, filling the silence with strokes on the chikari strings. At the same time he remained a traditional interpreter of great ragas such as Yaman, Todi and Darbari.

He also left his mark on film. He wrote the music for Satyajit Ray's Jalsaghar from 1958, for which he won a silver medal in Moscow, and for The Guru from 1969 and Kadambari from 1976. In 1951 he was probably the first Indian musician to play in England after independence.
artiest/vilayat-khan.listen: Listen to the music of Jalsaghar and notice how the sitar imitates the singing, gliding tone of a human voice. Can you hear where a note is bent after the string is plucked?

artiest/village-people.text:
Village People is an American disco group, conceived by the French producers Jacques Morali and Henri Belolo. After a series of hits in Europe, they went to New York in 1977 to conquer the American market. Morali, who played no instrument himself, wrote dance songs and found a singer in Victor Willis. The debut album Village People was aimed at the large gay audience of disco; the name referred to Greenwich Village, a well-known gay neighbourhood in New York. When the album caught on and there was demand for live shows, a group was put together around Willis, partly through an advertisement for macho, moustachioed types who could dance.

From 1978 the regular line-up consisted of six character types: a police officer, a Native American, a soldier, a motorcyclist in leather, a construction worker and a cowboy. With Macho Man, Y.M.C.A. (1978), In the Navy and Go West the group became world famous. Willis wrote the lyrics of the biggest hits. He left in 1979, and the film Can't Stop the Music (1980) was a flop. After that the group tried other singers and styles, without great success.

The music was cheerful disco with singalong choruses, played by a studio band under the direction of arranger Horace Ott. The costumes and the double-entendre lyrics played with images of American masculinity and gay fantasies. In this way Village People brought the gay culture of disco to a mass audience. In 2020 the Library of Congress added Y.M.C.A. to the National Recording Registry of culturally significant sound recordings.
artiest/village-people.listen: Listen to Y.M.C.A. and notice how the chorus is built for shouting along: short, separate letters that everyone can sing straight away. Also hear how the horns and the continuous disco beat drive the song forward.

artiest/vince-clarke.text:
Vince Clarke, born Vincent John Martin in 1960, grew up in Essex and learned violin and piano as a child. He was inspired by electronic groups such as Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark and the Human League. In 1980, with school friend Andy Fletcher and Martin Gore, he founded the band Composition of Sound, which became Depeche Mode with singer Dave Gahan. Clarke wrote the singles Dreaming of Me, New Life and Just Can't Get Enough from 1981 and left the group shortly afterwards. He did not like the public side of success, such as touring and interviews. Alan Wilder took his place.

He then formed the synth-pop duo Yazoo with singer Alison Moyet, called Yaz in America. Later he wrote for The Assembly. In 1985 he started Erasure, with singer Andy Bell. There Clarke makes the music, while Bell sings and does the talking on stage. The contrast is great: Clarke often stands almost motionless behind his keyboard, while Bell performs in a lively and exuberant manner. Erasure recorded more than two hundred songs and, by its own account, sold more than 28 million albums. Outside the group Clarke made solo albums such as Spectrum Pursuit Vehicle in 2001 and Songs of Silence in 2023.

In 2020 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Depeche Mode. His influence lies in short, clear pop songs built on synthesizers. In School of Rock, Erasure belongs to the 1980s, because Sometimes from 1986 showed that an acoustic guitar goes perfectly well with synthesizers.
artiest/vince-clarke.listen: Listen to Sometimes by Erasure. Notice the acoustic guitar among the synthesizers and how the two sounds do not get in each other's way.

artiest/vince-lawrence.text:
Vince Lawrence is an American producer and lyricist, born on 6 January 1964 in Chicago. He is regarded as one of the founders of house music. His father worked with Eddie Thomas of Curtom Records, and as a teenager Vince went on tour with funk musicians. There he saw synthesizers and keyboards at close quarters. He bought a Moog Prodigy and formed the band Z Factor, which in 1982 released the song (I Like to Do It In) Fast Cars.

In Chicago, at the teen club The Playground, Lawrence met the DJs Jesse Saunders and Farley Keith. Together they made On and On, which is seen as the first official house music. He designed the logo of Jes Say Records by hand and wrote lyrics for Funk U Up, which was the first house song to enter the Billboard charts. He also co-wrote Love Can't Turn Around with Daryl Pandy, in 1986 a hit in Britain that set off the house wave there.

Lawrence came up with the name Trax Records, when the pressing plant owner Larry Sherman decided to press the records for free in return for a share of the profits. He took the singles to clubs in Detroit and New York himself. With Marshall Jefferson he made the EP Virgo Trax. Later he founded Slang MusicGroup, which made music for bands, games, television and advertising. Lawrence shows that house began as a matter of teenagers with a synthesizer, a pressed record and a dance floor that was asking for it.
artiest/vince-lawrence.listen: Listen to On and On and notice how bare and mechanical the drum machine and the synthesizer line sound. Can you hear how a record made for the dance floor is above all about repetition and groove?

artiest/vincenzo-bellini.text:
Vincenzo Bellini was born in 1801 in Catania, in Sicily, into a musical family. His grandfather and father were organists and teachers. With a scholarship from the city he studied from 1819 at the conservatoire in Naples. He wrote his first opera for the conservatoire, in 1825. In Milan he broke through with Il pirata in 1827, followed by I Capuleti e i Montecchi in 1830, La sonnambula in 1831 and Norma, also in 1831. After a visit to London he wrote I puritani, which had its premiere in Paris in 1835 to great success. That same year he died in Puteaux, at the age of thirty-three.

Bellini belongs to bel canto, the Italian style of singing of the early nineteenth century. He wrote long, graceful melodies, which were ornamented without sounding complicated. For him, text and music belonged closely together. Verdi praised his extended melodies as unequalled, Wagner was impressed by the way he joined music and text, and Chopin and Liszt also admired him.

For pop history, Bellini matters as the source of the great melody that slowly unfolds. His operas are still performed, and Casta diva from Norma, through singers such as Maria Callas, has remained one of the best-known arias.
artiest/vincenzo-bellini.listen: Listen to Casta diva as performed by Maria Callas and notice how the melody rises in long arcs. Can you hear how the ornaments wrap around the main line like a kind of glow of light?

artiest/vinicius-de-moraes.text:
Vinícius de Moraes was born in 1913 in Rio de Janeiro and was above all a poet. He studied law, wrote his first collections of poems as early as 1933 and later became a diplomat, among other places in Los Angeles, Paris and Montevideo. His nickname was Poetinha, the little poet. He was a bohemian who married nine times and liked to talk about whisky.

His breakthrough in popular music came with the play Orfeu da Conceição from 1956, a Rio version of the Orpheus myth set against the backdrop of carnival. The pianist Antônio Carlos Jobim wrote the music for this play. The story was filmed as Black Orpheus, which in 1959 won an Oscar for best foreign-language film. De Moraes himself thought the film a failure. Together with Jobim he wrote songs that shaped bossa nova, including Garota de Ipanema. The album Canção do Amor Demais by Elizete Cardoso, full of songs by both, is regarded as a foundation of the genre.

In the 1960s he worked with Baden Powell on the Afro-sambas, the album Os afro-sambas from 1966. With Edu Lobo he wrote Arrastão for Elis Regina. In the 1970s came the regular collaboration with guitarist Toquinho, with whom he made many records and gave many performances. De Moraes had no great singing talent, a nasal baritone, but his lyrics made bossa nova into poetry. His work brought Brazilian song art to the world.
artiest/vinicius-de-moraes.listen: Listen to Garota de Ipanema in a version with Portuguese lyrics and notice the soft, almost whispered singing and the rhythm of the guitar. Can you hear how the melody moves calmly along with the poet's words?

artiest/violeta-parra.text: From 1952 Violeta Parra travelled through the Chilean countryside to collect and record old folk songs. She was also a visual artist: in 1964 she became the first Latin American artist to receive a solo exhibition at the Louvre, with her embroidered wall hangings. Her last album, Las últimas composiciones (1966), contains Gracias a la vida. She is regarded as a forerunner of the Nueva Canción, the politically engaged Chilean song.
artiest/violeta-parra.listen: Listen to Gracias a la vida and notice how simple the accompaniment is: a few chords on the charango, with the same grateful enumeration in every verse.

artiest/virgil-thomson.text:
Virgil Thomson was born in 1896 in Kansas City, Missouri, and was both a composer and a critic. He studied at Harvard, took an interest in the piano music of Erik Satie and lived in Paris from 1925 to 1940. There he studied with Nadia Boulanger and was influenced by members of Les Six. His most important friend was the writer Gertrude Stein. Together they made the opera Four Saints in Three Acts, performed in 1934 with an all-Black cast, and in 1947 The Mother of Us All. Thomson wove Baptist hymns, Gregorian chant and popular songs into his scores.

In 1936 he wrote the music for the documentary The Plow That Broke the Plains by director Pare Lorentz, commissioned by the American government. He used folk melodies and religious themes and later also made an orchestral suite of it. In 1938 came the film The River, and for Louisiana Story he received the Pulitzer Prize for music in 1949. From 1940 to 1954 he wrote for the New York Herald Tribune. He supported younger composers such as Ned Rorem and John Cage. He died in 1989.

Thomson played a major role in the emergence of what is called the American sound in classical music: simple, clear and with an open-air quality. That sound later returned in film music and in a great deal of American pop.
artiest/virgil-thomson.listen: Listen to Cattle from The Plow That Broke the Plains and notice the simple, open sound, which brings to mind wide open plains. Which instruments do you hear and how do they keep the piece light?

artiest/visage.text:
Visage was a British new wave band, started in 1978 in London by Midge Ure and Rusty Egan. Egan, together with Steve Strange, played records at club nights featuring music by David Bowie and Roxy Music, and was looking for new music to play. So Ure and Egan decided to make it themselves. Strange became the face and voice of the group. Keyboard player Billy Currie of Ultravox and three members of Magazine, guitarist John McGeoch, keyboard player Dave Formula and bassist Barry Adamson, completed the line-up. Visage was thus above all a studio project of musicians who also played in other bands.

Meanwhile Strange and Egan had moved their club nights to the Blitz Club in Covent Garden, the place where the New Romantics emerged. At the end of 1980 the album Visage and the single Fade to Grey were released. At the beginning of 1981 that song became a hit in England and reached number 1 in Germany and Switzerland. Mind of a Toy and the album The Anvil (1982) followed. Because the members were busy with their own bands, the group slowly fell apart. After the unsuccessful Beat Boy (1984), Visage came to an end. Strange later returned with new line-ups; he died in 2015.

Visage belongs to the core of the New Romantics: a movement of dressed-up clubgoers, striking clothing and make-up, and danceable electronic pop. The music leaned on synthesizers and electronic rhythms, with Strange's cool, detached voice. In this way Visage linked the London club scene directly with the hit parade.
artiest/visage.listen: Listen to Fade to Grey and notice the cool synthesizer sounds and the tight electronic rhythm. Also listen for the spoken French phrases between the English vocals.

artiest/vladimir-ashkenazy.text:
Vladimir Ashkenazy was born in 1937 in Gorky, today's Nizhny Novgorod. His father was a pianist and composer, his mother an actress. He began playing the piano at the age of six and studied at the Moscow Conservatoire. He came second at the Chopin Competition in Warsaw in 1955, won the Queen Elisabeth Competition in Brussels in 1956 and shared first prize at the Tchaikovsky Competition in 1962 with John Ogdon.

In 1963 he left the Soviet Union with his Icelandic wife and settled in London. Later he lived in Iceland and Switzerland. From 1963 he recorded for Decca. He committed an enormous repertoire to disc: the piano concertos of Mozart, Beethoven, Rachmaninoff and Prokofiev, the sonatas of Beethoven and Scriabin, the piano works of Chopin and Rachmaninoff and the twenty-four preludes and fugues of Shostakovich. With violinist Itzhak Perlman and cellist Lynn Harrell he made chamber music recordings with which he won Grammy Awards. In 1982 his own orchestration of Pictures at an Exhibition was released.

Halfway through his career Ashkenazy also began conducting. He led, among others, the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, the Czech Philharmonic Orchestra, the NHK Symphony Orchestra in Tokyo and the Sydney Symphony Orchestra. On stage he stood out by wearing a white polo-neck instead of white tie and tails. In 2020 he stopped performing. His flight from the Eastern Bloc and his broad, faithful recording work make him one of the most important pianists of the late twentieth century.
artiest/vladimir-ashkenazy.listen: Listen to his recording of Pictures at an Exhibition and notice the difference between the piano version and the orchestral version. Which passages sound more powerful on the piano?

artiest/vladimir-horowitz.text:
Vladimir Horowitz was born in 1903 in Kyiv, then part of the Russian Empire. His mother, herself a pianist, gave him his first lessons, and from 1912 he studied at the Kyiv Conservatoire. In 1925 he left the Soviet Union, officially to study in Berlin, in reality with the plan of not returning. His debut at Carnegie Hall in 1928, with Tchaikovsky's first piano concerto under Thomas Beecham, caused great excitement. In 1933 he married Wanda Toscanini, the daughter of the conductor Arturo Toscanini, with whom he often performed. He settled in the United States and became an American citizen.

Horowitz recorded for, among others, RCA Victor, Columbia and Deutsche Grammophon. His 1932 recording of Liszt's Sonata in B minor is for many the benchmark. He played mainly Romantic repertoire, with a great deal of Rachmaninoff, Scriabin and Chopin, but also intimate music by Schumann, Scarlatti and Clementi. His technique, tone colour and the tension in the hall made him famous.

His career had long interruptions because of doubt and depression. Between 1953 and 1965 he did not perform, and in 1965 he returned at Carnegie Hall. In 1986 he played in Moscow for the first time since 1925, a concert with both musical and political significance. He died in 1989 in New York. Horowitz showed that a pianist with nothing but a grand piano and a hall could sweep an audience away, almost like a pop star.
artiest/vladimir-horowitz.listen: Listen to his recording of Liszt's Sonata in B minor and notice the contrast between thundering passages and very soft, transparent moments. Can you hear how he builds tension without rushing?

artiest/vladimir-spivakov.text:
Vladimir Spivakov is a Russian violinist and conductor, born in 1944 in Ufa. He studied with Yuri Yankelevich at the Moscow Conservatoire and is regarded as one of the leading violinists of his generation. His name is above all associated with the Moscow Virtuosi, a chamber orchestra that he led.

In the 1980s and 1990s many recordings appeared on which he plays or conducts. Among them are Four Seasons with two violin concertos by Vivaldi, a Carmen Suite from 1987 and performances with the English Chamber Orchestra. In this way he built up a broad classical repertoire, from Baroque to the twentieth century.

Later Spivakov became artistic director and principal conductor of the Russian National Philharmonic Orchestra. He also conducted the music for the animated film The Ugly Duckling from 2010 by Garri Bardin. In 1982 he received the Lenin Komsomol Prize and in 2006 he became a UNESCO Artist for Peace. His position in relation to Russian politics is controversial: in 2014 he supported a letter defending the policy on Crimea, and in 2022 he signed, together with other Russian artists, a letter against the invasion of Ukraine. Spivakov shows how a soloist can choose the chamber orchestra as a permanent conversation partner and so remain violinist and conductor at the same time.
artiest/vladimir-spivakov.listen: Listen to his recording of Four Seasons and notice how the solo violin relates to the string orchestra. Can you hear how the soloist determines the movement of the ensemble?

artiest/volker-bertelmann.text:
Volker Bertelmann, born in 1966 in Kreuztal, is a German composer and pianist who performs mainly under the name Hauschka. He had piano lessons as a child, formed a rock band at fourteen and briefly studied medicine and business administration in Cologne before choosing music. In 1992 he formed the hip hop duo God's Favorite Dog with his cousin, which released an album on Epic and split up in 1995. After that he began writing piano music in Düsseldorf. He borrowed his stage name from the Bohemian composer Vincenz Hauschka.

The sound of Hauschka is that of the prepared piano. On The Prepared Piano from 2005 he wedged leather, felt and rubber between the strings, wrapped aluminium foil around the hammers and placed small objects on the strings. As a result, the piano sometimes sounds like a percussion instrument. His first album, Substantial, was released in 2004. Ferndorf in 2008, Foreign Landscapes in 2010, Salon des Amateurs in 2011 and What If in 2017 followed, among others. In 2012 he made the album Silfra with the violinist Hilary Hahn.

Since 2012 Bertelmann has also written film music. With Dustin O'Halloran he composed Lion, which was nominated for an Oscar. He also wrote for, among others, Adrift, The Old Guard, Ammonite and Stowaway. For All Quiet on the Western Front from 2022 he won an Oscar and a BAFTA. Bertelmann proves that an experimental pianist who comes from the club world can bridge the gap to the cinema.
artiest/volker-bertelmann.listen: Listen to a piece from the album The Prepared Piano or What If and notice the sounds that do not sound like ordinary piano notes. Can you hear the hammers, foil and objects on the strings, and how they form a rhythm?

artiest/volker-bertelmann-hauschka.text: Volker Bertelmann was born in 1966 in Kreuztal and grew up in Ferndorf. He discovered the piano at the age of eight in church and had ten years of classical piano lessons. At first he studied medicine and business administration in Cologne. From 1992 he worked as a musician. Under the name Hauschka he makes music for prepared piano: between the strings he places leather, felt, rubber and other materials. This gives the piano a different, sometimes percussive sound. With Dustin O'Halloran he wrote Lion (2016), which earned an Oscar nomination. For Im Westen nichts Neues (2022) he received an Oscar and a BAFTA. Conclave (2024) was also nominated for an Oscar.
artiest/volker-bertelmann-hauschka.listen: In Im Westen nichts Neues, listen to the harsh three-note motif that returns like a mechanical alarm, and in Conclave to the nervous, bowed strings.

artiest/vox-luminis.text:
Vox Luminis is a Belgian vocal ensemble for early music, led by Lionel Meunier. The ensemble was founded in 2004; its first performance was a concert at the IMEP music academy in Namur. In 2009 it settled in that city. The line-up varies: the core consists of eight to thirteen singers and two continuo players, and for certain projects instrumentalists are added. The ensemble sings mainly vocal music from Italy, England and Germany from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. It strives for a coherent vocal colour, without hiding the personality of the individual singers.

The international breakthrough came in 2012 with the recording of Heinrich Schütz's Musicalische Exequien for the label Ricercar. That record won, among other awards, a Gramophone Award and an International Classical Music Award. Other recordings include Samuel Scheidt's Sacræ Cantiones, English Royal Funeral Music from 2013, Brockes-Passion from 2014, Motets of the Bach family, Actus Tragicus with cantatas by Bach and Requiems by Fux and Kerll from 2016. In 2018 the record Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott won a BBC Music Magazine award, and in 2019 the ensemble again received a Gramophone Award, for Buxtehude: Abendmusiken.

Vox Luminis performs in major concert halls and festivals throughout Europe. The ensemble is among the most important players in the contemporary practice of early music and brings choral music from before the Classical period to a broad audience.
artiest/vox-luminis.listen: Listen to Schütz's Musicalische Exequien and notice how the voices merge into a single sound and then emerge again separately. Can you hear how few instruments are needed to make the funeral music weighty?

artiest/w-c-handy.text:
William Christopher Handy was born in 1873 in Florence, Alabama. His father, a preacher, considered musical instruments the work of the devil, but Handy secretly bought a guitar and later a cornet. He worked as a teacher, played in bands and at the age of twenty-three became bandleader of Mahara's Colored Minstrels. In 1903 he heard a man playing guitar with a knife as a slide at a station in Tutwiler, Mississippi, a moment he later described as formative. In 1909 he settled in Memphis and played in clubs on Beale Street.

Handy did not invent the blues, but he was one of the first to publish music in blues form. His first hit was The Memphis Blues, originally a campaign song for mayoral candidate Edward Crump, published as sheet music in 1912. Saint Louis Blues followed in 1914, then Beale Street Blues and Yellow Dog Blues. In 1917 he moved his music publishing company to New York. He used the three-line stanza, the blue notes and the room for improvisation by the singer. He himself said that he was setting down existing folk music.

Bands that played jazz took up his songs enthusiastically, as a result of which many of them became jazz standards. His publishing company also published work by other Black composers. Handy called himself the Father of the Blues. He went blind after an accident in 1943 and died in 1958 in New York, where an estimated 150,000 people attended his funeral. Handy brought the blues from a regional folk art to the general public, on paper and on record.
artiest/w-c-handy.listen: Listen to a recording of Saint Louis Blues and notice the tango rhythm at the start and the transition to the blues stanza. Can you hear how one rhythmic mood abruptly gives way to the other?

artiest/wadada-leo-smith.text:
Wadada Leo Smith is an American trumpeter and composer, born in 1941 in Leland, Mississippi. He began on drums, mellophone and horn before choosing the trumpet, and played in R&B groups. In 1967 he became a member of the AACM in Chicago, the collective of innovative jazz musicians. There, with Leroy Jenkins and Anthony Braxton, he formed the trio Creative Construction Company. In 1971 he started his own label, Kabell, and founded the group New Dalta Ahkri with, among others, Henry Threadgill, Anthony Davis and Oliver Lake. In the mid-1980s he became a Rastafarian and adopted the name Wadada.

Smith prefers to call his work creative music rather than jazz. He often sets down his compositions in a graphic notation of his own, Ankhrasmation, which he developed in 1970. Besides trumpet and flugelhorn he plays instruments from other cultures, such as the koto, the kalimba and the atenteben, a Ghanaian bamboo flute. On early records such as Creative Music 1 from 1971 and Silence from 1974 he explores space, silence and abstract sounds. In 1998 he made Yo, Miles! with guitarist Henry Kaiser, a tribute to the electric period of Miles Davis.

With his Golden Quartet, at first with Jack DeJohnette, Anthony Davis and Malachi Favors, he recorded several albums. His major work Ten Freedom Summers, about the American civil rights movement, was released in 2012 and was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for music in 2013. Smith has also taught, among other places at CalArts. He shows how the free jazz of the AACM grew into a world of notation and sound of its own.
artiest/wadada-leo-smith.listen: Listen to his trumpet playing on a recording by the Golden Quartet and notice the long notes, the silences and the role of the drums. Can you hear how a single note can carry tension?

artiest/waldjinah.text:
Waldjinah is an Indonesian singer, born in 1945 in Surakarta, also called Solo, in Central Java. She was the tenth child in her family. Her mother sold food at the market and her father worked as a painter in a batik factory, where she heard the traditional Javanese songs that inspired her. At secondary school she became interested in kroncong. In 1958 she won a singing competition held by the radio station Radio Republik Indonesia in Surakarta. That was the start of her career as a professional singer. In 1960, at a national competition in Jakarta, she was named the singer with the most potential.

Her best-known song is Walang Kekek from 1968, which made Javanese kroncong known throughout Indonesia. Her backing band was called Orkes Keroncong Bintang Surakarta, and her son Ary Mulyono, himself an instrumentalist, now leads that band. She is said to have recorded 200 albums and more than 1,500 songs and worked with Gesang Martohartono and Ismail Marzuki.

Kroncong is an Indonesian style of music with ukulele-like strings, violin and flute, a soft, swaying accompaniment and melodious singing. Waldjinah showed that the Javanese variant, the langgam Jawa, could reach a large audience. She is one of the best-known and best-loved traditional singers in the country.
artiest/waldjinah.listen: Listen to Walang Kekek and notice how the voice floats freely above the light, swaying accompaniment. Can you hear the playful, almost dancing character of the melody?

artiest/walter-becker.text:
Walter Becker was an American musician, songwriter and producer, and, together with Donald Fagen, the core of Steely Dan. He was born in 1950 in Queens, New York. He began on saxophone and switched to guitar, on which a boy from the neighbourhood taught him the blues. At Bard College Fagen heard him play in a coffeehouse and thought it sounded very professional. Together they started a student band and then tried to make a living in Brooklyn as a songwriting duo. For a time they played in the backing band of Jay and the Americans.

In 1971 they moved to Los Angeles, where they became songwriters at ABC Records and started Steely Dan. Fagen sang and played keyboards, Becker played bass and later guitar. From 1974 the band stopped touring and worked only in the studio, with different top musicians for each album. Albums such as Pretzel Logic (1974), Aja (1977) and Gaucho (1980) combined pop songs with jazz chords, tight grooves and ironic, cryptic lyrics. Becker and Fagen wrote everything together and were notorious for their perfectionism in the studio.

The years around Gaucho were hard for Becker, with a drug addiction and an accident, and in 1981 the duo stopped. Becker moved to Hawaii, got off drugs and became a producer, among others for China Crisis and Rickie Lee Jones. In 1993 Steely Dan got back together. The album Two Against Nature (2000) won four Grammys. Becker also made two solo albums. He died in 2017.
artiest/walter-becker.listen: Listen to Peg by Steely Dan, from the 1977 album Aja. Notice the rich jazz chords beneath an ordinary pop melody and the tight, smooth accompaniment of the studio musicians.

artiest/walter-brown.text:
Walter Brown was born in 1917 in Dallas, Texas, and was an American blues singer of the blues shouter type. He first sang in cafés in Kansas City and in 1941 became the singer of pianist Jay McShann's orchestra. The young saxophonist Charlie Parker also played in that band that year. Brown stayed with the group until 1944.

In April 1941 the orchestra recorded in Dallas for Decca. Among the songs produced there were Hootie Blues and Confessin' the Blues. Brown wrote the latter together with McShann, and it became the band's biggest hit and made the bandleader's name known nationwide. It has since been covered by, among others, Wynonie Harris, B.B. King, Little Walter, Chuck Berry and The Rolling Stones. Brown was replaced in 1944 by Jimmy Witherspoon.

His solo career remained without great success. In 1947 he recorded with Tiny Grimes's sextet a version of Open the Door, Richard, which, because of its lyrics, regarded as obscene, was refused by most radio stations and quickly withdrawn. He went on recording for labels such as King, Signature and Mercury and briefly returned to McShann in 1949. In 1956 he died in Lawton, Oklahoma, as a result of addiction. Walter Brown matters above all as the voice of Kansas City blues in the early 1940s, the singing partner of an orchestra in which bebop was making its first appearance.
artiest/walter-brown.listen: Listen to Confessin' the Blues by Jay McShann with Walter Brown and notice the loose, talking style of singing above the swinging accompaniment. Can you hear how the band lets him sing and then answers with short riffs?
